title: Dropped Name
passages:
Dawn bled pale across Anza's ore stub, the kind of light that shows every crack in the rail ties and every oil stain on the concrete. The blank rig was already a shrinking coal on the northbound line, its hand lamp a wobbling orange eye retreating toward the Blank. No transponder pulse. No board entry. Just eleven warm canisters and a flame in a crew box window, rolling north on stolen momentum.

Kass walked the empty siding with their boots kicking up rail dust, the pedal-rail shed yawning dark behind them. Anza's chain had gone green again at 08:00 — Teodoro's trick with Voss's name — but the node still tasted like held breath. Clearances stripped. Resupply frozen until the re-list took. Nour's chalk still held forty names under an amber chain that hadn't been amber since morning.

A flash of white in the gray dust. Kass stopped, boot heel grinding it flat.

A coast ticket. Heavy card stock, folded sharp into thirds the way you fold something you mean to keep. The bought name on the face meant nothing — *J. RENNER, TRANSIT CLASS, VALID THROUGH WINTER* — but the graphite thumbprint smudged into the corner, and the deep crease from a coat pocket's hard edge: those were Miko's. Kass had watched Miko fold tickets that way a dozen times. Pocket, unfold, check, pocket. The rhythm of someone who didn't trust anything to stay put.

Kass picked it up with two fingers, turned it over. Blank back. No stamp. No punch. If the ticket was here, its owner wasn't. And Miko had three of these things under three different names, paid for with cargo weight Kass didn't want to know about.

The wind shifted, carrying the rig's diesel ghost south. The hand lamp bobbed once, steady as a breath held.

Kass slipped the ticket into their own pocket, coat crease matching coat crease, and kept walking the siding toward the pedal-rail shed. The ore line stretched north, empty and patient. Culvert Nine sat penciled on Anza's board in Saul's careful hand — proposed, not live. A dead pump station with a live storeroom and a woman who'd marked it in her own name.

Kass's badge caught the light, thin and bent at one corner. They had a tally card cleared, a glove with a cut palm, and a chip match made but not read out. They had a thread they wouldn't drop.

The pedal-rail waited in its shed, chain dry, bearing ready to shriek. Past the first node, there was no one left to call.

The relay shop's side door stuck on its track, metal grinding metal. Kass shouldered it open and stepped into the cool dark, letting the door swing shut behind them. Dawn light sliced through the high windows, catching dust motes and the green chain marker snapped into its slot on the resupply board.

*CHAIN RESTORED — VOSS RE-LISTED 08:00 — RESUPPLY LIVE*

Teodoro's handwriting, cramped and precise. The board was black-painted steel, chalk lines ruled in white. Shift roster at the top, resupply notes below. Kass read down the names with the ticket burning in their coat pocket.

Nour — Shift 1 Lead. Doan — *CLEARANCE WITHDRAWN* scratched red beside it. Teodoro — Reader Two. Wren Cardoso — *SHOP HAND — COUNTERSIGNED 2244*, fresh chalk still dusting the letters.

Fifth line down: *MIKO — RESUPPLY LOADER*.

The checkmark box beside it was scraped clean. Not erased — *scraped*, like someone had taken a knife to it. The chalk outline of the mark remained, ghost-white against black steel. The shift had formed. The shift had left. Miko's name stayed on the board, but her body hadn't shown up for the roll call.

Kass's thumb found the ticket's folded edge through the wool. *J. Renner*. One of three names Miko had bought. Three tickets, three chances at the coast. She'd used none of them to leave.

Below the roster, in a different hand — pencil, careful print, pressed hard enough to groove the steel:

*PROPOSED RESUPPLY: CULVERT NINE*

No time stamp. No reader initials. No green chain marker beside it. Just Saul's handwriting and a dead station name. Culvert Nine. A pump station that hadn't pumped in fifteen years, its storeroom sealed and its jaw rusted shut — until Odessa Brill had marked it in her own name and the receiving jaw had started reading cargo again.

Eleven warm canisters on a blank rig. Nour's eleven short seals, struck full at Anza's jaw, paid out to Brill's storeroom to keep Anza eating through winter. The rig had pulled out at 06:47 by Teodoro's log. Two hours fourteen minutes ago. The ore line grade was steady but long — two and a half hours to Culvert Nine's switch if the rig held speed, three if it didn't.

The hand lamp had been burning in the crew box window. Steady. Fed. Someone was on that rig, watching the flame.

Kass stood between the scraped slot and the penciled name. The ticket in their pocket. The glove with its cut palm at their hip. The tally card cleared in their bag.

The rig was hours ahead. The canisters were headed for a jaw that faulted on skims. And Miko was on that rig — or she wasn't, and the ticket in Kass's pocket was the only proof she'd ever been there at all.

The shop door banged open behind them.
